title: Intelligent Delivery: Making Every Unit of Compute Serve Better Ads
abstract: Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding where to allocate it to get the best outcome for the entire system. We built Intelligent Delivery, an ML-driven system that allocates resources across the serving stack toward the system-wide optimum. It has delivered ~10% incremental ranking performance on top of model and system advancements since 2017. We’re sharing a few of Intelligent Delivery’s capabilities: how we build ML models to predict the marginal utility of compute, multi-layered mechanisms to move resources across the system, and how we increasingly leverage agentic AI to continuously detect and respond to system shifts. As frontier ads ranking systems advance toward larger models, broader candidate sets, and richer delivery architectures, they also place greater demands on serving efficiency. Compute resources do not scale at the rate that models and system complexity do. The challenge is not just how to build more powerful models, but how to operate them efficiently across a heterogeneous system, with finite serving capacity, and under a tight latency budget. We recently shared how we put idle inference capacity to work . This post covers how we decide where each unit of compute goes to achieve globally optimal system efficiency. Intelligent Delivery is our approach to the problem, and it has contributed an additional ~10% improvement in ads ranking performance on top of model and system advancements across major surfaces, from 2017 through the first half of 2026. It introduces an ML-driven, increasingly AI-operated adaptive optimization layer that continuously directs resources toward the requests, models, hardware fleets, and ranking stages with the highest marginal utility. This helps us run advanced ads ranking models efficiently in production, getting more out of every unit of compute to serve better ads for people who use our apps and services. The Goal and What Makes It Difficult One of our goals is to create a delivery system that continuously converges on its global optimum, regardless of how user behavior changes, models evolve, and the serving stack grows more complex. Three fundamental properties of ads delivery systems make this challenging: The marginal impact of compute is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent: The same additional unit of compute can generate very different returns depending on the product surface, user intent, candidate quality, and system state. Request-aware signals alone are not sufficient; allocating well means estimating, for every request, the return on every available tunable system parameter, where each knob behaves differently at each stage of the funnel. We need to produce a per-request result calculation across a vast decision space within milliseconds. Local optimality does not translate to global optimality: Result estimation is just the start; the serving stack must also be dynamically controllable. Ads delivery spans multi-stage ranking , hundreds of models, generations of hardware, and many data centers. Resources cannot be shifted freely and reliably across these boundaries without adaptive controls that account for complex dependencies throughout the stack. The global optimum is a moving target: The optimization landscape is continuously shifting. Every new model, hardware generation, or new architecture changes the landscape and can invalidate previously optimal allocation decisions. The system needs to adapt quickly enough to retain its optimality. Intelligent Delivery includes three capabilities, each designed to address one of these fundamental system challenges. title: Your Algorithm: Giving People More Ways to Personalize Facebook Recommendations
abstract: Your algorithm is a suite of AI-powered tools that makes Facebook recommendations more transparent and steerable, with a single editable view of the interests that shape Feed and Reels. We’re sharing how Your algorithm turns people’s natural language preferences into responsive recommendations, and how LLMs are tailored to specific tasks within the system. Traditionally, the recommendation systems behind what people see on Facebook have learned from implicit engagement signals. While this allows them to scale well, it also means they adapt slowly and capture little nuance. But what if people could interact directly with the algorithms that rank and recommend what they see to instantly make their recommendations more personal and customized? Your algorithm is an end-to-end system that addresses the limitations of adaptability and nuance in recommendations. This new suite of AI-powered tools lets people on Facebook state, in their own words, what they want to see in their Feed and Reels. By tasking a collection of large language models (LLMs) with understanding, storing, and tracking people’s stated preferences along with their user behavior, we’ve created a recommendation system that responds to people’s preferences and adjusts the content they see. An Overview of the Your Algorithm System Architecture The Your algorithm page has three parts (Figure 1): At the top, a one-sentence Lately Summary that describes recent viewing activity. Below it are two lists: “Interested In,” prefilled with interests inferred from past activity. “Not Interested In,” capturing topics the user has explicitly marked as not interested, or has X-ed out or hidden on Facebook. People can use the interface to add interests (using natural language), move them between lists, or remove them. Every change applies responsively to both Feed and Reels, and will further update as the person gives feedback on individual posts. Figure 1: The Your algorithm page. Your algorithm system has several components that cover the full lifecycle of a preference, from inferring and validating it to applying it in ranking and delivery (Figure 2). Profile generation builds the initial interest profile. Preference management validates each change, enriches it with the signals ranking needs, and saves it to a single store that both Feed and Reels read, ensuring that the preferences shown on the page are the same ones used in ranking. Ranking applies the “Interested In” and “Not Interested In” lists throughout the funnel. Delivery optimization helps each change take effect more responsively. Figure 2: An overview of the Your algorithm system. From Preferences Into Recommendations Turning a stated preference into recommendations poses three distinct problems. An interest added to Interested In needs to deliver relevant content quickly, without crowding out everything else. An interest added to Not Interested In needs to hold reliably, even though topics are fuzzy and any single filter misses some matches. And both need to take effect responsively, even when the next recommendations were cached before the change. Your algorithm addresses each problem with dedicated logic across the recommendation funnel, from retrieval through reranking to the device (Figure 3). Interested In: Surfacing New Interests Without Flooding Each interest in Interested In drives four dedicated retrieval sources. Two find matching content directly (through search and through clusters of closely related topics), and two extend reach through the content graph and item-to-item similarity. Retrieving explicitly for each interest ensures enough relevant candidates for downstream ranking. This is important because, without it, content about a brand-new interest might never enter the ranking pipeline at all. Candidates that pass a relevance check, which compares the meaning of the interest with each candidate, receive a promotion in late-stage ranking so they can compete alongside other content. title: How We Built TLX: A Hardware-Native GPU Compiler for Production ML at Scale
abstract: Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX) , is an extension to Triton that helps engineers optimize GPU performance while preserving Triton’s productive programming model. TLX introduces explicit warp-group and cluster-level orchestration, letting developers adopt new hardware capabilities without sacrificing velocity. TLX has demonstrated performance improvements in RecSys training, RecSys inference, and large-scale LLM pretraining. Modern GPU architectures increasingly rely on execution-oriented features such as warp specialization, asynchronous memory movement, tensor memory, and cluster-level execution to optimize their performance. But these same features also expose a growing gap between low-level programming models for control and high-level programming models for productivity. To bridge this gap, we built Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), an extension that gives engineers explicit control over GPU execution while preserving Triton’s productive programming model. Today, TLX powers production workloads across Meta, from AI training to large-scale LLM pretraining, enabling engineers to adopt new hardware capabilities quickly without sacrificing developer velocity. Across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, TLX is pushing the frontier of GPU performance — combining state-of-the-art kernels with explicit execution orchestration and model-aware fusion to deliver end-to-end improvements beyond what standalone libraries can achieve. From AI Models to GPU Kernels To understand where TLX fits, it helps to trace the path from an AI model to the GPU instructions that ultimately execute it. At Meta, machine learning (ML) workloads are built on a common software stack centered around PyTorch. Model code is transformed through graph capture, optimization, compilation, and lowering before eventually becoming GPU kernels running across large accelerator fleets. Over the past several years, Triton has evolved from an experimental kernel language into a foundational component of this stack. A significant share of production GPU kernels — both compiler-generated and hand-optimized — are now implemented in Triton. Improvements at this layer can therefore propagate broadly across training and inference workloads, making kernel performance an increasingly important lever for improving end-to-end system efficiency. Figure 1: Normalized kernel count growth at Meta over a 10-month period (start = 1.0 in month 1). Over this period, Triton kernel count grew ~3.8x compared with ~2.0x for CUDA, reflecting Triton’s rapidly expanding role in Meta’s GPU software stack. This shift has also changed who writes kernels. Kernel optimization is no longer the exclusive domain of GPU specialists. ML engineers routinely profile workloads, identify bottlenecks, and optimize the hottest kernels through autotuning, fusion, memory-layout improvements, or algorithmic restructuring. Triton’s productivity allows many of these iterations to happen in hours rather than days, enabling engineers to stay close to the model-development workflow. As a result, GPU kernel development has increasingly become part of the standard optimization toolkit for ML engineers. Triton already provides a productive foundation for many memory-bound workloads through fusion and compiler-managed memory-access optimizations. Building on these strengths, TLX addresses a complementary challenge: coordinating execution groups, asynchronous data movement, and shared resources on modern GPUs. The Problem: When Hardware Evolves Faster Than Programming Models While Triton dramatically improved developer productivity, modern GPU architectures have evolved in ways that place increasing emphasis on execution orchestration rather than computation alone. NVIDIA’s Hopper introduced warp specialization and the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA). title: Microsoft Research Focus – Edition #98
abstract: What’s new in research? In this edition of Microsoft Research Focus , based on the Research Focus newsletter (opens in new tab) , host Anson Ho shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from bringing AI-powered universal translation closer to reality and solving a 31-year-old mathematical challenge to making AI coding agents faster and more efficient. Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next. I’m Anson Ho, and these are some of the latest advances we’re tracking. Coming up in this edition: how AI is bringing the possibility of a universal translator closer to reality; a breakthrough that solves a 31-year-old mathematical challenge; a new approach to make AI coding agents faster and more efficient; and more. Here’s what’s new. [MUSIC FADES] Internship: Growing expertise, building community At the Microsoft Research lab in Tokyo, research intern Lilika Makabe found opportunities to grow her expertise while helping to shape a new research community. Makabe joined the lab with a background in computer vision and worked alongside researchers exploring robotics and physical intelligence, AI systems that can interpret information and act in the physical world. Her experience highlights how research internships can offer more than technical training. Through hands-on experimentation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and everyday conversations with colleagues from different backgrounds, Makabe expanded her research perspective while contributing to the lab’s growing community. You can read about her experience on the Microsoft Research blog. [TRANSITION MUSIC] Breaking the language barrier with AI For decades, science fiction has imagined a world where language barriers no longer stand in the way of communication. For example, in 1967, Star Trek introduced the fictional Universal Translator. Now, advances in AI are bringing that possibility closer to reality. In a new conversation, Microsoft Applied Science Manager Jinyu Li explores how AI is advancing the prospect of communication across languages, the progress researchers have made, and the challenges that remain. To learn more, catch the full episode of the podcast Our Digital Life , available to listen or watch on YouTube and podcast platforms. New research has resolved the conjecture. This removes a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The breakthrough establishes a universal principle for log-concave distributions: simple flat cuts can identify their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
abstract: Microsoft researchers have discovered “Lazarus,” a backdoor technique that can reprogram dormant neurons in an AI model, causing an otherwise normal AI agent to execute malicious commands when a hidden trigger appears. The threat is especially serious for AI agents with tool or terminal access. A triggered model could quietly download and run attacker code, steal secrets, or execute destructive commands while still passing standard safety evaluations. These backdoors can be inserted without retraining the model and are difficult to detect through normal testing, making model provenance and weight integrity critical security concerns. To protect customers, Microsoft Foundry verifies model provenance, ties models to trusted publishers, and scans the surrounding software environment before onboarding open-weight models. Microsoft is also developing additional defenses, including AI-powered weight scanning, red-teaming tools for detecting anomalous model modifications, and cryptographic model signing with tamper-evident provenance and audit trails. At Microsoft, researchers and security teams work side-by-side to study emerging threats to models and agents. Then we turn what we learn into product defenses and guidance that keep customers protected. More broadly, Lazarus is an example of a practice that should become routine: AI agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them. Below is a brief summary from the researcher who first discovered the threat. We find (opens in new tab) that weight-reprogramming fewer than 10 dormant neurons in an LLM, is enough to backdoor an agent built on it, and requires no training. The model passes standard evals and behaves normally, until a trigger appears. The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent—in the middle of an ordinary task—emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code. The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it. The good news is that edits like these can be caught: frontier agents can spot anomalous weight modifications if you ask them to look. But no scan can prove beyond any doubt that a model is safe. Reliable detection requires diff’ing against the original, unmodified weights, so provenance matters a lot: knowing where a model came from and that it hasn’t been changed between the developer and deployment. Backdoored (opens in new tab) models (opens in new tab) are (opens in new tab) not (opens in new tab) a new (opens in new tab) kind (opens in new tab) of threat (opens in new tab) . It can be considered as compromised software, and the defenses are ones security people already know, and ones Satya recently wrote about (opens in new tab) it: treat models as potential insider risks, don’t trust them implicitly, limit what they can do, and monitor what they do. What Microsoft does today. Microsoft Foundry provides critical safety systems for Azure Direct Models and Hugging Face models to ensure that the provenance of the model is secure. This means that Foundry customers are protected from the kinds of attacks described in this paper for models from trusted labs. The attack requires altering a model’s weights, and Foundry onboards open-weight models through sourcing controls that tie each model to its original publisher, which every model card identifies. Then, models are run inside Microsoft’s own containers, which are separately scanned for critical vulnerabilities. These controls cover where a model came from and the software around it. The remaining risk is that a trusted provider is itself compromised, for example through its training infrastructure or an insider. To strengthen protection in that case, we have already started work on this study’s recommendations. title: Using mathematics to validate network configurations
abstract: Corporations, banks, hospitals, and academic institutions all rely on wide-area networks (WANs) to connect their local networks across geographic regions. Within a WAN, however, it’s often necessary to isolate different computational resources from each other: for example, coding environments used to test new website features should remain separate from active websites. Customers rely on such isolation — or segmentation — to help protect sensitive data; a single misconfiguration of segmentation rules could allow traffic to reach unintended parts of a network or allow data to cross organizational boundaries. Historically, validating network segmentation has involved mapping the network by sending packets through it. The size and complexity of modern networks, however, make it impractical to build a complete map this way, so organizations instead rely on a sampling process that sends packets through only portions of the network. The result is that network segmentation is rarely validated exhaustively. By using Tiros, Amazon Web Services’ automated-reasoning tool for analyzing network connectivity, we’re offering an alternative to dynamic sampling that is designed to validate segmentation across all modeled paths. Previously, Tiros had been used in customer-facing services such as Amazon Inspector, VPC Reachability Analyzer, and Network Access Analyzer. These services focus on reachability, or determining whether some sequence of valid requests leads from one network resource to another. Our key insight is that if we can determine the reachable paths in a network, then we can also identify the absence of paths between particular resources. Fundamentally, automated segmentation validation is a static process: it examines a network without relying on dynamic packet traffic. Using Tiros, we can analyze the topology of a deployed network as frequently as every hour. These analyses provide a mathematical demonstration that the topological description aligns with our isolation specifications. Automated segmentation validation In modern networking, a virtual network sits on top of the physical network of servers and wires and other components. Segmentation is achieved through logical rules and routing policies rather than physical isolation of network hardware. We consider the case in which an Amazon Web Services (AWS) customer is using the AWS Cloud WAN service to configure and deploy a large organizational WAN. To validate network segmentation using Tiros, we first collect the customer’s Cloud WAN configuration from route tables, “attachments” (which are like a virtual cable within the network), and policy documents. Specialized software converts these configurations into logical propositions that describe network behavior. Now, we have a configuration that’s expressed logically, so that automated reasoning tools can analyze it. Then we ask Tiros, “Which attachments can reach which attachments with which destination IPs?” Tiros generates the satisfying assignments it can derive from the network description, each of which corresponds to a path. Our system checks that no path exists between segments that the policy declares should be off limits from each other. If actual reachability matches the expected segmentation, the validation check succeeds; if they differ, the system alerts an operator. When the company updates its website, it does so from a replica of the public-facing website inside the development environment within Cloud WAN. The production environment needs to be strictly contained, so that tests and changes not yet ready for deployment don’t reach the live website, which is maintained in the separate production environment. title: Mitra-v2: Scaling synthetic pretraining for tabular foundation models
abstract: Much of the data that businesses run on lives in tables: the rows might represent customers, transactions, or interactions, and their “attributes” are listed in the columns. Predicting missing attributes — such as likelihood of customer retention or how much demand to expect next week — is one of the most common machine learning tasks in industry. The standard tools for this job, such as gradient-boosted decision trees, produce models tailored to specific tables. Every new table means choosing an algorithm, engineering features, tuning hyperparameters, and setting up a processing pipeline. Tabular foundation models promise to end that cycle: one pretrained model reads the labeled rows of a previously unseen table and predicts the rest, with no training run in-between. Last year we introduced Mitra, a tabular foundation model pretrained entirely on synthetic tables. It worked well on small and mid-sized tables but ran out of room on large ones, wide ones, and problems with many classes. Today we're introducing Mitra-v2, the second generation of the model, for both classification and regression. We describe it in a technical report, and we've released versions fine-tuned for both classification and regression, along with the inference and fine-tuning code, under the Apache-2.0 license on Hugging Face. Amazon Connect Customer, which provides agentic-AI systems for core business functions, led the effort. Amazon Connect Customer is adopting Mitra-v2 for prediction on structured business and customer-experience data, such as estimating how likely a business-relevant event is to occur given a customer's interaction history and operational context. On TabArena, a public benchmark of 51 real-world datasets, Mitra-v2 leads the single-model field. It produces a better result than Mitra-v1 on 32 of the 33 datasets where both models run natively, and it completes all 51 datasets within the benchmark's one-hour budget, which Mitra-v1 failed to do on more than a third of them. On ScoringBench, a public benchmark for regression models that predict a range of likely outcomes rather than a single number, fine-tuned Mitra-v2 ranks first. Synthetic pretraining A large language model is pretrained on huge volumes of data, so when you give it a few examples in a prompt, it can generalize from them with no additional training. Tabular foundation models work the same way. We pretrain Mitra-v2 on millions of synthetic prediction problems, and at deployment time the labeled rows of a real table serve as the examples. The model reads them and predicts the unlabeled rows, a technique called in-context learning. Every pretraining table is synthetic: we use no real data, and in particular, no customer data. The model learns general principles about how columns relate to one another rather than the contents of any real dataset. The lesson of the original Mitra was that the quality and diversity of those synthetic tables are central to how well the model generalizes. Mitra-v2 takes that lesson further. The architecture is unchanged: a Transformer that attends both across the rows of a table and across its columns. What has changed is the size of the examples the model sees during pretraining. Mitra-v2 is pretrained on tables with 10 times as many rows and roughly three times as many columns as those used to train Mitra-v1, so it has seen tables the size of the ones businesses actually use. We also added a new family of synthetic tables. To train the original Mitra, we generated tables from structural causal models (SCMs), which are graphs of cause-and-effect relationships between columns, and from tree-based models like the ones data scientists fit in practice. Mitra-v2's new hybrid SCM prior builds a single causal graph in which each relationship can be a small neural network, a decision tree, a smooth function drawn from a Gaussian process, or a time-dependent autoregressive process, so one synthetic table can carry the mix of relationships found in real

title: Deploy frontier AI models on AWS Trainium with SGLang-Neuron
abstract: Today, Amazon announced that SGLang-Neuron is publicly available and can be accessed through an AWS Deep Learning Container, released by RadixArk in collaboration with Annapurna Labs. With SGLang-Neuron, you can serve models and generate reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts with SGLang on AWS Trainium using the same SGLang interface you use today. Trainium is a portfolio of AWS AI chips that delivers strong economics for AI training and inference at scale. Now, running SGLang on Trainium follows the SGLang workflow you already know: you launch models through SGLang’s server interface and invoke the endpoint using the same generation APIs. Underneath that interface, SGLang-Neuron runs on native PyTorch. With its out-of-tree plugin design, Trainium support and SGLang core develop independently and iterate faster. How SGLang runs on Trainium SGLang-Neuron is an out-of-tree plugin that connects SGLang with AWS Trainium. Installing the plugin registers the neuron platform through SGLang’s plugin entry points, and setting SGLANG_PLATFORM=neuron selects it when the server starts. SGLang core continues to provide the API server, request lifecycle, RadixAttention, and prefix-cache bookkeeping. The plugin implements the Trainium-specific models, attention, mixture of experts (MoE), and the graph runner. Figure 1: SGLang-Neuron on AWS Trainium TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device. SGLang-Neuron uses standard PyTorch operations for the model execution path and incorporates kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for performance. It compiles these operations and kernels into executable programs using torch.compile , which the graph runner prepares and executes during serving. SGLang-Neuron also supports PD disaggregation . In this configuration, a prefill server computes the prompt KV cache and transfers it to a decode server using NIXL over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) . The decode server then generates the remaining tokens. Each server still uses SGLang’s scheduler and request lifecycle, while the plugin manages the Trainium execution and KV-cache transfer path. Serving models on AWS Trainium using SGLang-Neuron To follow this walkthrough, you use a Trainium3 Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance with a pytorch-inference-sglang-neuronx container. Here are the steps: Start the container. docker run --rm -it \ --privileged --ipc=host \ -v /path/to/work:/work \ public.ecr.aws/neuron/pytorch-inference-sglang-neuron:v0.1.0-neuron-py314-sdk-2.33.0-ubuntu26.04 \ /bin/bash Launch the SGLang model server inside the container. SGLANG_PLATFORM=neuron \ python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path openai/gpt-oss-120b \ --tp-size 8 \ --ep-size 8 \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \ --context-length 10240 \ --chunked-prefill-size 8192 \ --max-running-requests 64 \ --max-total-tokens 655360 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 30000 Send a request to the model server. curl -s http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "model": "openai/gpt-oss-120b", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Explain why the sky appears blue."} ], "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 128 }' For additional information, please see the SGLang-Neuron getting started guide for setup instructions, and explore the repository documentation for supported models, features, and validated configurations. Conclusion SGLang-Neuron brings SGLang’s familiar serving workflow to AWS Trainium through native PyTorch. You can get started by launching the SGLang-Neuron container and following the quickstart to serve a supported model. Try it with your workloads, contribute through the project repository, and share feedback to help shape future model and feature support. title: How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: At Natera , a leader in cell-free DNA (cfDNA) testing, keeping lab instruments up and running is critical, because equipment downtime disrupts sample processing. Natera’s lab engineering team, led by Ariel Jirau worked with AWS to build SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system for lab operations. This post walks through how the Natera team built an agentic AI system for lab operations using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that captures and deploys institutional knowledge at scale. It describes the full architecture, from knowledge base construction to automated system deployment and evaluation, so you can apply the same patterns to your own operational workflows. SWARM delivers about 130x faster first response time and 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets, giving engineers immediate access to institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives. The challenge: Knowledge continuity Natera’s lab operations rely on a wide range of precision instruments spanning multiple equipment families, each with its own failure modes, vendor documentation, and resolution patterns. The service engineering team responsible for maintaining this infrastructure is organized around deep individual expertise rather than standardized playbooks. When a senior technician who had spent years diagnosing a particular instrument family departed, the institutional knowledge they carried was effectively lost. No system existed to capture, organize, or deploy that expertise at scale. With over 65 tickets per day across three Jira queues and an average first response time of 17.4 hours, instrument downtime delayed lab samples and patient reporting. Hiring more engineers couldn’t keep pace. SWARM had to respond in minutes, deliver accurate diagnostics across a wide range of equipment types, and improve continuously through a structured evaluation loop. Why Natera chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore The Natera team chose to build SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a fully managed, extensible service by AWS designed to build, deploy, connect, secure, and operate AI agents at scale. Three core requirements drove the decision: Autonomous processing of high-volume support tickets without human intervention. Deep integration with existing operational tools such as Jira and Confluence. Built-in security and observability (encryption, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) integration, and distributed tracing) without requiring the team to build and maintain custom infrastructure. “We needed a managed runtime that would let us focus engineering effort on diagnostic accuracy rather than infrastructure plumbing—AgentCore gave us that, along with built-in identity management and the flexibility to swap models without rewriting agent logic,” Jirau said. AgentCore provides native integration with services including Amazon DynamoDB , a fully managed NoSQL database service, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) , and AWS X-Ray , a capability of Amazon CloudWatch. How SWARM works: Two agents, one skill library SWARM uses two complementary runtimes sharing a single skill library. The swarm-agent autonomously generates structured diagnostic reports before an engineer opens a ticket, while engineers use swarm-hive to interact in real time, upload images, and explore alternative troubleshooting paths. “The system does not replace engineers—it gives them access to the full depth of institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives,” Jirau said. Four layers connect the architecture: The event layer routes Jira tickets through Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS. The agent layer hosts swarm-agent, swarm-hive, and the skill library, and delivers diagnostic reports back to engineers. The context layer draws on vendor manuals, historical tickets, and operational data. The observability and delivery layer captures traces, logs, and metrics. title: Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost
abstract: Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing after you tune prompts and application logic. Request-level choices can still change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied to them. Cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and maxTokens can affect cost without changing your model or prompt. Each choice depends on the model and workload. This post shows how we tested each choice and how to verify its effect from response metadata, logs, and billing data. To try these settings yourself, start with the Amazon Bedrock Samples notebooks Mixed TTL Caching and Tenant Isolation with Prompt Caching . For maxTokens and reasoning effort, see the 01-low-effort folder of the sample-code-for-genai-cost-management-workshop GitHub repo. Each sample sets its own model ID, so change it, and the inference parameters, to match the model you call. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Models at a glance . For broader decisions such as model selection, batch inference, routing, and distillation, see Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock . Where inference cost comes from Every Amazon Bedrock response carries usage metadata. Input and output tokens bill at the rate for the model and tier that served the request. Cache reads and writes use separate token counters, and reasoning tokens count as output tokens. Prompt cache duration Repeated system instructions, tool definitions, or reference context can be processed again when the cache expires before the next request. The Prompt caching for faster model inference guide lists 5-minute and 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) values for supported Anthropic models. It also lists a 30-minute minimum TTL for supported GPT-5.6 models. Support and API fields depend on the model, so check the current support matrix before selecting a duration. For supported models, Amazon Bedrock also offers implicit prompt caching , which attempts to reuse eligible prompt prefixes without cache controls in your request. Because implicit caching is best effort and doesn’t guarantee a cache hit, the duration choices in this section apply to explicit caching. This Converse API signature requests a 1-hour entry on models that support it: { "cachePoint": { "type": "default", "ttl": "1h" } } For supported Anthropic models, InvokeModel places the same ttl value in cache_control . A longer duration is not automatically cheaper. The Amazon Bedrock Pricing page lists separate rates for 5-minute writes, 1-hour writes, and cache reads. For Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock, a 5-minute write costs 1.25 times the input rate. A 1-hour write costs 2 times, and a cache read costs 0.1 times. These rates set the break-even, assuming each request reuses the exact prefix and each cache read refreshes the TTL. A 5-minute cache pays back on the first reuse within 5 minutes. When requests for the same prefix arrive more than 5 minutes apart, it rewrites at 1.25 times on every request. The 1-hour cache is then cheaper from the second request within the hour. Cache rates and checkpoint minimums differ by model. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page and the prompt caching guide for the model you call. Rerun the comparison for your model, then confirm it with cache read and write tokens after rollout. Keep stable content before dynamic content, meet the model’s checkpoint minimum, and use on-demand inference because prompt caching doesn’t work with batch inference. Changing a cached prefix, including a system instruction or tool definition, causes a miss and a new write. Checkpoints are evaluated in the order tools, system, then messages, so a change in an earlier section also invalidates the later ones. Version prompts that change often so each version gets its own cache entry. We ran six calls on Claude Sonnet 5 with a 1-hour checkpoint, changing the system prompt once and the tool definition once. Each change produced zero cache reads and a new write. AWS describes

title: Tokenomics at scale: Track and cap Amazon Bedrock spend per IAM principal with CUR 2.0 and AWS Budgets
abstract: Generative AI spend is hard to attribute. Before an organization expands AI access, CFOs and CTOs usually want three answers: what do we spend per person or per team, can we cap it, and how much work does it take to get there. In our previous post, Tokenomics at Scale: How Jamf Built Real-Time Spend Enforcement for Amazon Bedrock , we explained a custom enforcement loop built on AWS IAM Identity Center , Amazon Athena over Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs , and AWS Lambda . This approach gives near-real-time control, but it requires code you then own and operate. This post shows how to get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code to write for the common case. The approach relies on three things: IAM principal attribution , which Amazon Bedrock records automatically; AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) 2.0 or AWS Cost Explorer for reporting; and AWS Budgets with budget actions for enforcement. By the end, you will have per-identity cost reporting and an automatic guardrail that restricts Amazon Bedrock access when a threshold is crossed. Solution overview The solution has three parts: attribute, report, and enforce. Attribute. Amazon Bedrock captures the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal identity, the IAM user or role , for every inference request. This happens automatically, with no change to your Amazon Bedrock model inference calls. If several people share one role, you add per-user detail with session tags passed at role assumption time. If each person or application has its own role, principal tags on the role are enough. Report. Activate those tags as cost allocation tags, then read the data either in Cost Explorer for a console-only view, or in a CUR 2.0 data export for detailed line-item analysis and SQL queries. Enforce. Create an AWS Budget scoped to Amazon Bedrock and filtered to one identity or tag value, then attach a budget action that applies a Deny IAM policy when the threshold is crossed. The following sections show each part in more detail, alongside the implementation steps. Prerequisites To deploy this solution, you need: An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock model access enabled. Permissions to tag IAM principal , activate cost allocation tags , create data exports , and create budgets and budget actions. Amazon Bedrock accessed through IAM roles or IAM users. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with appropriate credentials. A CUR 2.0 data export and an Amazon Simple Storage Service ( Amazon S3 ) bucket to receive it. (optional, for detailed line-item analysis) . Amazon Athena. (optional, for querying the export) . AWS Billing Console access is managed separately from most IAM permissions. Confirm you have it before starting. Walkthrough Before configuring anything, check what you already have. Amazon Bedrock records caller identity for every inference request automatically. Open Cost Explorer, filter Service to Amazon Bedrock, and group by the available identity or tag dimension. For accounts where each application or person already uses a distinct IAM role, this may be all the visibility you need. To configure additional visibility: Step 1 gives you identity-level visibility. Steps 2 through 4 add tag dimensions and detailed reporting. Step 5 adds enforcement. Step 1: Decide how identity maps to your users How you tag depends on how your IAM principals are organized. One role per person or per application. Attach principal tags directly to each IAM role or user. These are static and apply to every request from that principal. Use the IAM console, or the AWS CLI: aws iam tag-role \ --role-name BedrockDeveloperRole-alice \ --tags Key=user,Value=alice@example.com Key=team,Value=platform Key=CostCenter,Value=CC-1001 A shared role used by several people, or a gateway. title: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Part 1 of this series built the operating model that controls Amazon Bedrock spend: attribution with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal tags and Cost and Usage Report 2.0, observability with model invocation logging, enforcement at three tiers, and a review cadence. That layer answers who spent it, and you can stop them. It can’t tell you whether the spend was well spent. This post answers two questions that Part 1 deliberately left open. First: Why is this workflow expensive? The answer requires thinking in cost per task, not cost per token. Second: Is the agent better than the humans were? The answer requires baselines, controlled experiments, and a scorecard tied to decisions. In this post, you learn a framework for calculating true model cost (including four hidden cost drivers that the pricing page doesn’t show), techniques for reducing cost per task through caching, routing, and output constraints, and a discipline for measuring agent ROI with human baselines, holdout experiments, and a five-dimension scorecard. This post is written for two audiences: the application and platform engineers who own the optimization levers, and the product owners and FinOps partners who need to justify agent spend to leadership. Cost per task, not cost per token Price per token invites quick comparison, but it doesn’t reflect what you actually pay. The published rate reflects the cost of a single token. Your bill reflects the cost of completing a task. A task is one complete unit of work your application asks a model to do: resolve one support email, extract fields from one invoice, or answer one user question. A task runs from the request through to a usable result, however many model calls it takes. The lower-priced model might not be the cheaper one to run. A cheaper model might fragment your text into more tokens, pad responses with filler, misread your tool schema and loop through corrections, or burn thousands of reasoning tokens before answering. None of these costs appear on the Bedrock pricing page . The four hidden cost drivers Four model characteristics determine what that published rate actually costs you on your workload. Tokenizer efficiency A token isn’t a word, and it is not equal across models. Every model family uses a different tokenizer and vocabulary. The same text, code, or JSON payload splits into different token counts. If Model A’s list price is 15 percent lower but its tokenizer needs 40 percent more tokens for your data (common with structured schemas and numerical arrays), Model B is cheaper. The gap widens for non-English text: many tokenizers fragment non-Latin scripts into two to three times more tokens than the equivalent English. Output alignment and verbosity Output tokens commonly cost 3–5x more than input tokens (the ratio varies by family. Refer to the Bedrock pricing page ). A model that ignores formatting constraints like “return only raw JSON” makes you pay that output premium for filler words. A model that follows formatting instructions closely saves money by generating fewer of these more expensive output tokens. Agentic loop efficiency Agentic workflows change the cost math entirely. Tool use (function calling) lets a model invoke external functions, requiring a multi-turn loop: analyze the prompt, decide to call a tool, wait for the observation, generate an answer. Each turn re-sends the full conversation history and tool results as input tokens. A model that takes four turns (each one re-sending a larger context payload) costs far more than one that finishes in a single pass. Reasoning overhead Many models support extended thinking , working through a chain of thought before the visible answer. Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens, so a model that thinks for 2,000 tokens before a 200-token answer bills you for 2,200. Some models redact the reasoning while still charging for it. Start with reasoning turned off and enable it only when benchmarks show a quality gap that justifies

title: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM
abstract: Developers want AI coding assistants with minimal setup. With a large language model (LLM) gateway and LiteLLM, they can quickly access foundation models (FMs) available on Amazon Bedrock while you gain visibility and usage control. Platform teams need to monitor latency and errors, finance teams need to attribute inference costs to teams and projects, and security teams need consistent access controls. An LLM gateway can help address these needs by providing a centrally managed access point to the models that power coding assistants. In this post, we show how to build a self-service LLM gateway using Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles with LiteLLM running on AWS Fargate to abstract Amazon Bedrock behind an OpenAI-compatible API. With this pattern, developers can access foundation models through a single API with a dedicated key while you gain per-user cost controls and model performance observability. By the end, you will understand the pattern well enough to build your own version from the illustrative snippets and AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs. This post uses Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku models for example purposes. For a list of models and availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . This LLM gateway pattern follows a straightforward request flow from the developer, through the LiteLLM layer, to Amazon Bedrock and the underlying FM. The following diagram illustrates the production topology behind that flow. For simplicity, we don’t cover the addition of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, such as content filtering and grounding, but you would normally include appropriate responsible AI controls before deploying to production. A developer’s OpenAI-compatible client reaches the LLM gateway through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB). It authenticates to LiteLLM on Fargate with a per-user API key. Behind that, the request draws on Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) (PostgreSQL) for virtual-key and spend state. It also interacts with Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache, and AWS Secrets Manager for secrets. LiteLLM then ultimately invokes Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles using a scoped AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) task role. Amazon CloudWatch captures requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) metrics and the quota alarm. Figure 1: LLM gateway architecture (production topology) The architecture consists of these core components: LiteLLM on AWS Fargate : LiteLLM provides a proxy that exposes an OpenAI-compatible API. We run it on an AWS Fargate task with target-tracking Auto Scaling on CPU utilization. Developers point their tools at this endpoint and don’t interact with Amazon Bedrock directly. Self-service portal : LiteLLM includes a lightweight portal for admin and developer self-service. This web app can integrate with your corporate single sign-on (SSO). Using the portal, operations engineers set the spend policy while developers self-provision API keys within those parameters. Persistent and cache storage : LiteLLM uses Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey for non-persistent response caching. It also coordinates rate-limiting across AWS Fargate tasks. A separate Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL) database is the database of record for persistent state such as API key metadata and spend tracking. Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles : Each model (such as Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku) gets its own inference profile, which you manage using the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). With this, you get per-model quota isolation and a clean abstraction layer between LiteLLM’s configuration and the model versioning of Amazon Bedrock. Langfuse : Open source LLM observability for prompt-level telemetry, latency tracking, and debugging. It complements the infrastructure-level metrics of Amazon CloudWatch with application-level insight. By using an OpenAI-compatible protocol, developers can co

title: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime
abstract: AI agents have moved past one-off prompts. They now run multi-step workloads for hours at a time. The length of task that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months ( METR ), and 40 percent of large enterprises are scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago ( McKinsey ). As agents run longer and with more autonomy, the focus shifts from what agents can do to how securely, reliably, and economically they can operate at scale. Agents do more than traditional software: they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce new security and infrastructure demands, making strong isolation essential for production deployments. Every agent session needs a secure, isolated environment. But delivering that isolation at scale introduces a fundamental challenge: balancing performance, cost, and efficiency. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs. On-demand environments reduce wasted capacity but introduce cold-start latency, delaying agent execution. Neither approach scales efficiently without trade-offs. As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex, expensive, and unpredictable. The challenge is evident. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they can’t yet trust and govern their agents ( Deloitte ). Scaling agents shouldn’t mean choosing between security, speed, and cost. The next generation of agent infrastructure must deliver strong isolation with fast startup times, elastic scaling, and usage-based economics. Because as AI agents move into production, secure execution shouldn’t be the bottleneck. It should be the foundation that makes scale possible. The fastest path to production should also be the safest one. The next generation AgentCore runtime We built Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help developers build, connect, and optimize agents securely at scale. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the managed compute layer. It gives developers a fully managed environment to deploy and run agents without building or maintaining infrastructure. Since launching, our customers have been pushing their agents into increasingly complex workloads. As those workloads grow, so do the demands on the execution environment: more compute, more flexible billing, and trust boundaries that extend to data, not only compute. Agents reach production at scale if the infrastructure underneath was built for both scale and speed. Today we’re announcing updates to AgentCore runtime that meet those demands. The core guarantee stands: every session runs in its own hardware-isolated Firecracker micro virtual machine (MicroVM), with its own identity, policy, and audit trail. These updates expand what’s possible within that guarantee. Sessions now start up to 15x faster, scale to 4x more compute, and run up to 68% more efficiently, with the isolation boundary fully intact. Here’s what’s new. Run bigger workloads without waiting longer to start Teams building increasingly advanced agents asked for more flexibility: the ability to scale memory and compute within the isolated session to match the demands of their workloads. From large codebase compilations to browser-driven workflows to local model inference, the execution environment needs to keep pace. Sessions now scale 4x compared to the previous version, up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, with support for container images up to 10 GB. Sessions start in under 2 seconds, independent of image size and concurrency. You no longer need warm pools and pre-provisioned clusters to manage cold starts. “AgentCore Runtime lets us run AI-driven development at scale. title: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent
abstract: With a customer-managed knowledge base on Amazon Bedrock , you provision and scale the vector store, tune the embedding model and index settings, and plan capacity for each new data source. The migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps you migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base . Managed Knowledge Base takes over that work and adds new retrieval capabilities, and your team keeps control of the content and the application that uses it. Moving a production knowledge base means your team maps its configuration, creates the replacement, ingests content, updates the application’s retrieval call, and validates retrieval before switching traffic. To help, we added a knowledge base migration guide to the amazon-bedrock skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS . The guide gives your coding agent the context to plan the migration with you, starting with read-only discovery and a plan you review line by line. On your approval, the agent creates the new knowledge base and its data sources alongside the original, or writes a migrated infrastructure as code (IaC) template for your pipeline. Ingestion and updating your application’s Retrieve calls stay with you, and your agent can walk you through both. In this post, we explain why we recommend the move and how the migration guide works, review the prerequisites, install the skill, plan a migration, update the application’s retrieval call, and validate retrieval before cutover. Why move to Managed Knowledge Base We recommend Managed Knowledge Base because it balances ease of use, retrieval accuracy, and cost. AWS runs the store With a Managed Knowledge Base, Amazon Bedrock handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval, and the store scales automatically as your content grows. Hybrid search, which combines keyword and semantic matching, is always on, with no index to configure. The knowledge base includes a managed embedding model, a managed reranker, and a built-in parser for multimodal file types. You can still bring your own Amazon Bedrock embedding model when you create the knowledge base. On each retrieval request, you choose the managed reranker, an Amazon Bedrock reranking model, or no reranking. The managed reranker requires the managed embedding model. Built-in capabilities Managed Knowledge Base includes capabilities you’d otherwise build yourself: Native connectors ingest content directly from sources such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Microsoft SharePoint, and Atlassian Confluence. For the current list, see supported connectors . After the first full sync, later syncs pick up only changes, on demand or on a schedule. The Managed Knowledge Base includes a deletion safeguard to help protect against accidental bulk removal of indexed content. Access control list (ACL) awareness ingests document permissions with the content, so retrieval returns only what the signed-in user can access. For connectors that support it, such as Microsoft SharePoint and Atlassian Confluence, a real-time check against the source also catches permission changes since the last sync. ACL awareness doesn’t authenticate users, so your application must verify and pass the user’s identity. Agentic retrieval answers questions that a single search can’t by handling multi-part questions and retrieving iteratively. It can search more than one knowledge base in a single request. Integration with AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes your knowledge base as a target. Any client that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can then query the knowledge base, and the gateway handles authentication. Resource-based policies let applications in other AWS accounts use one team’s knowledge base. Scope each policy to the specific roles that call the knowledge base, and grant only the actions they use, such as bedrock:Retrieve . Agentic retrieval, AgentCore Gateway integration, and resource-based policies are not available on customer-managed knowledge bases. Fo

title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
abstract: Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides. The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use. While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running. In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test. The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project , and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks. In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A , we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. This post builds on that foundation with cross-framework interoperability, cross-organizational trust boundaries, and OAuth in both directions. Solution overview Three agents run in two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider. The A2A protocol connects them, with OAuth authentication in both directions. Each account has its own Amazon Cognito user pool, so each side authenticates with its own identity provider. Figure 1: A2A agents across an enterprise account and a SaaS provider account During onboarding, the enterprise and the SaaS provider exchange only public values, such as identity provider URLs, client IDs, scopes, and endpoint URLs. Each side then trusts tokens from the other side’s user pool, and no secrets are shared. After onboarding, each request follows these steps: The enterprise app gets an access token from the enterprise’s Amazon Cognito user pool. The app sends a question over HTTPS to the user API in Amazon API Gateway, then polls for the answer. Amazon API Gateway forwards the request privately, through a VPC link and an internal Network Load Balancer, to the Enterprise Orchestrator, a LangChain agent. When its model decides that the question needs a compliance scan, the orchestrator gets its own token from the enterprise user pool, using a client secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager . The orchestrator sends an A2A request to the compliance SaaS agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, using the skill it read from the agent’s Agent Card at startup. The compliance agent checks the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card at the callback URL registered at onboarding, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own pool.

title: Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools
abstract: More enterprises are building AI agents into their daily work, and a common pattern is an agent that searches internal documents to compose its answers. A single organization might soon run hundreds of agents, each connected to many data sources and tools. This raises a question. When an agent searches on behalf of a user, can you make sure that it uses only the information that user is allowed to see? Consider AnyCompany, a fictional company that builds an internal assistant shared by all employees. An employee in department A asks, “Compare my department’s business plan with the notice to all departments, and list the initiatives that are behind schedule.” The agent writes its own search queries and keeps searching internal documents until it has enough information. Employees in department B ask the same assistant the same question. If the application doesn’t scope searches to each user, the department B business plan can end up in an answer to an employee in department A. If you replace the departments with customer companies, the same problem occurs in a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) architecture where multiple customers share one assistant and knowledge base. Controlling access to multi-tenant data through this agent is harder than in traditional applications. In a traditional application, the application code determines who the signed-in user is and searches with that user’s permissions. In an agent, a large language model (LLM) decides at runtime which tool to call and with which arguments. If a search tool takes “who to search as” as an argument, the LLM decides that value too. A prompt injection or an LLM error might then make the agent search as a different employee. In this post, we build an internal assistant for AnyCompany. All employees share the same agent and knowledge base, yet each employee can search only the documents they’re allowed to view. We use Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base as the search backend and expose it to the agent as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The design principle is to not let the LLM decide who the user is. Instead, trusted code decides, based on information that your identity provider has verified. On top of that, we add independent layers of defense in case that mechanism has a bug or is bypassed. Solution overview Managed Knowledge Base has a feature called ACL awareness . When a search request includes a user context ( userContext ) with the user’s email in userId , the knowledge base returns only the documents that user is allowed to view. If your application calls the search API directly, the application code sets the search scope from the authentication result. Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base shows this pattern. When you expose the knowledge base as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway, however, userContext becomes a tool argument, and the LLM constructs its value. Neither the gateway nor the knowledge base verifies that this value belongs to the authenticated user. This solution injects verified user attributes into tool calls at the tool layer (AgentCore Gateway). It then scopes the search by those attributes at the resource layer (Managed Knowledge Base). The sample stores three documents in a single knowledge base: business plans for department A and department B, and a notice shared with all departments. Two users, user-a in department A and user-b in department B, search through the same agent. The following diagram shows the architecture. title: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC
abstract: Over the past year, AI agents have moved from exploration into engineering. Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge. A successful demo can show what an agent is capable of. Before release, the team needs to answer a further question: “ Is this agent ready for production? ” The person responsible for that decision needs evidence that the agent meets the agreed requirements. To make that decision consistently, teams need a repeatable, affordable way to assess the agent’s current behavior and whether the latest change has improved it. In traditional software development, teams answer these questions with unit tests, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), and passing builds. Those mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient for agents, for three reasons, each requiring additional checks. This post explains these three properties and presents a measured case where an aggregate metric hides a coverage problem. It then introduces the Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC): one lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change. A note on terminology: Throughout this post, gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against. Business owners approve this standard as the basis for acceptance decisions. 1. Three properties of agents that require additional engineering practices Conventional software testing and CI/CD still apply to agents, but three properties require additional checks. First, agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths. Second, changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal. Third, model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior. Table 1 summarizes the engineering practices needed to address each property. Table 1. What each property invalidates, and what it requires instead. Property The conventional answer Why it falls short What Agent DLC requires Non-determinism One assertion per case in CI Measures a single sample of a distribution. Passes and fails for reasons unrelated to your change Run each example k times. Judge on pass rate and failure distribution Prompts are source code Review the diff, approve the change Behavior can’t be read off the text of a prompt Every prompt, tool, retrieval, and memory change is versioned with an evaluation attached, and the lineage is kept Dependencies move on their own Pin versions, validate on upgrade Doesn’t fire because nothing in your repository changed Re-run the standard on a schedule and alert on deviations from the baseline 2. A measured example: High retrieval precision can hide missing information The following example shows how the choice of metrics affects diagnosis. We built a reference implementation to exercise the method end to end: an internal policy assistant answering HR policy questions over a document knowledge base. We chose a narrow, well-scoped domain to make the evaluation and diagnosis straightforward to follow. The following results were measured on this reference implementation. It isn’t a customer outcome and it isn’t a benchmark result. The accompanying AWS Samples repository includes infrastructure deployment, the HR agent, custom evaluators, and scripts for baseline evaluation and prompt-change re-evaluation ( 09-run-eval.sh and 10-optimize-prompt.sh ). It also includes optional checks for judge repeatability, model comparison, cost, and latency. The scripts reproduce the workflow. Scores can vary across runs and repository versions. title: Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI
abstract: Java teams have established JVM tooling, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, and operational patterns, yet taking AI agents from prototype to production is hard: agent frameworks do not solve scalability, governance, security, and operational concerns by default. Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI close those gaps, so Java teams can build autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and APIs, and maintain context across multi-turn conversations. Agentic AI is moving beyond prompt-response interactions toward autonomous systems that execute complex multi-step tasks. Java remains one of the widely used programming languages in enterprise software. Teams have existing CI/CD pipelines, operational expertise, and established patterns built around the JVM. Spring AI brings AI capabilities to the JVM through familiar Spring patterns: auto-configuration, dependency injection, and composable advisors. Developers can build AI agents using the same idioms they use for REST APIs, security, and data access. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. With AgentCore, you can build, deploy, and operate AI agents at scale. It is framework-agnostic and model-agnostic: you bring your preferred agent framework and foundation model (FM). With AgentCore, you can access the production infrastructure you need: managed runtime, memory, browser automation, code execution, and identity management. In this post, we show you how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock with spring-ai-agentcore . We explore the key implementation patterns for two systems. The first is a single-agent travel assistant that demonstrates tool calling and memory. The second is a multi-agent intelligent document processing (IDP) system that shows how specialist agents, a rules engine, and alerting work together. Prerequisites To follow along with this walkthrough, you need the following: Java – JDK 21 (required) Spring Boot – 4.1 (with Spring AI 2.0 and spring-ai-agentcore 2.0) Maven – 3.9+. Node.js – 18+ (for the React frontend) Terraform – 1.5+. Docker – with Buildx for multi-architecture builds. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) – v2, configured with credentials. An AWS account . What makes a system an agent A chat completion call can generate text, but it can’t decide what to do next, reach into external systems, or remember what happened yesterday. An agent can, because it unites three capabilities: Planning – Given a goal, the model breaks it into steps, prioritizes them, and revises the plan as new information arrives. Tool use – Beyond generating text, the model can select and invoke external functions such as APIs, databases, and code interpreters to act in the world. Memory – Context carries across turns (short-term) and across sessions (long-term), so each decision builds on what came before. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application has limited tool use (retrieval) but no planning loop. An agent has all three, operating in a goal-directed loop until the task is complete or it determines it cannot proceed. The following diagram shows these capabilities in an end-to-end agentic pipeline, from request to grounded answer. Figure 1: Agentic reference architecture. A request flows through the runtime, guardrails, classification, a specialist agent, tools, the foundation model, memory, rules, and human review to a grounded answer, with resilience and observability as cross-cutting concerns The pipeline has 11 stages. A client submits a document and question. The request passes through a runtime gateway for authentication and rate limiting, then input guardrails screen for harmful content. A router classifies the document and routes it to a specialist agent, which plans its workflow and calls tools, the Amazon Bedrock foundation model, memory, and a rules engine as needed.
