title: Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification
abstract: When reviewing code, you start with a diff. You wouldn’t compare two 3,000-line files by eye and hope to spot every change. Formal policies can be even harder to compare because a textual diff often highlights syntactic changes that don’t affect meaning. Reorder two conjuncts, swap the arguments of an equality, or use an equivalent predicate, and much of the file might appear changed. A real change in behavior, such as an Or where the requirement says and , can get lost in that noise. A semantic diff shows what two policies have in common and where they disagree. The open source engine used in this post computes this diff using anti-unification , which finds a most specific common pattern for two expressions. Plotkin’s 1970 paper gives the classical formulation. The engine works over an e-graph, which keeps track of expressions known to be equal. We supply the algebraic laws and domain rules that justify those equalities, such as equating an external destination with one that isn’t internal. The result shows the shared parts once and keeps both versions of each differing part for review. If no differences remain, the policies are equivalent under those laws and rules. When the rules or the search are incomplete, a remaining difference might reflect an equivalence the engine has not found. One use case is autoformalization. Autoformalization translates natural language into a formal language. Suppose you want to turn requirements into SMT-LIB , the standard input language for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers such as Z3 and cvc5, or into Cedar or Dogwood to control authorization in your software system. A large language model (LLM) generates the formal artifact from the prose. The model writes the artifact. It plays no part in computing the diff. Run the model twice, and it might produce two different formalizations, with no ground truth to identify the correct one. A semantic diff shows where they agree and where they differ. Generate more candidates by varying the model, prompt, or sampling temperature. Comparing them shows which parts stay the same and which vary. Review the varying parts first. Requirements can also become OpenShell sandbox policies or Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions. OpenShell uses YAML to describe an agent’s filesystem and network access. CEL is embedded in applications to evaluate expressions, including policy conditions. These languages and formats differ in what they express, but translations into any of them can disagree about a condition, a scope, or an event. The following table gives illustrative disagreements: Language or format Policy focus Example disagreement Cedar Who can perform an action on a resource, under which conditions. One translation requires ownership and approval. Another accepts either. Dogwood Authorization involving the current request and recent event history. One translation checks a successful prior response. Another checks a request event. OpenShell policies An agent’s filesystem and network access, including rules for particular binaries. One translation permits repository-scoped GET . Another permits organization-scoped POST . CEL Conditions evaluated over inputs supplied by a host application. One translation requires production for both allowed ports. Another requires it for only one. In each worked example, we compare translations of the same requirement within one policy context. We encode the relevant syntax as terms and declare the equalities used in the comparison. The engine reads these encodings. It doesn’t import native policies from the four formats. The idea is a formal-methods analogue of semantic entropy , described by Farquhar et al. in Nature (2024). That approach samples several natural-language answers, clusters those that entail one another, and reports a single number. For formal outputs, anti-unification preserves more information. It identifies the shared structure and each divergence instead of returning only a score. Countere

title: Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
abstract: Silent data corruption (SDC) happens when hardware, such as a GPU, returns a wrong but plausible number and raises no error. In distributed training, the wrong number can flow into the gradients and weights of every replica. Loss can still look normal for hours, and by the time a team notices an unexplained divergence or a weaker model, the compute is spent. It happens at scale: during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on up to 16K H100 GPUs, Meta attributed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions to silent data corruption, and those were only the cases that interrupted the job and were traced to SDC. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod already replaces nodes that report a fault: the health-monitoring agent watches for GPU errors, deep health checks stress-test nodes, and automatic node recovery swaps out bad hardware. SDC slips past all of these features, because the hardware never reports anything. Detection has to come from the training job itself. In this post, we add three checks to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop to detect SDC. When a check fires, we map the suspect rank to its node, contain the corruption, and have SageMaker HyperPod replace the node. Each check covers a different place where a fault can land: A non-finite gradient check catches NaN, Inf, and overflow in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step it happens, and NaN or Inf that the gradient all-reduce introduces. A ring replay audit catches finite wrong values. On audit steps, every GPU recomputes a micro-batch from another node and compares the loss bit for bit and the gradients by fingerprint. A weight fingerprint comparison catches corruption in the optimizer step and in stored weights, by comparing every replica’s weights after the update. We tested the checks with software-injected faults on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs), and repeated every test on three instances, the minimum the checks need. The full code of this solution is available in the accompanying GitHub repository . How silent data corruption happens and why the usual checks miss it SDC comes from manufacturing defects (marginal transistors that slip past vendor screening) and silicon aging in a specific compute unit, most often a multiply-accumulate lane in a tensor core, which is exactly the hardware model training hammers. That marginal circuit computes correctly most of the time and wrong only under stress: high temperature, voltage droop, or specific operand patterns. Because the arithmetic logic path has no ECC or parity (unlike memory), the wrong result, say 4.0001 instead of 4.0000, is never flagged, and it flows through activations and gradients into every replica’s weights. The reason it is so hard to catch is that SDC is in the compute path, and every integrity check you already have guards a different boundary : Check What it guards Why it misses SDC ECC memory Catches bit flips in memory, not wrong math. There is no ECC on a tensor-core result. Xid errors (NVRM) GPU driver/hardware faults The GPU raises an Xid when it detects a fault. SDC by definition raises none, so nothing lands in /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/ HMA logs. DCGM deep health check hardware faults Misses defects that need your workload’s operands, thermal state, or timing. Runs on an idle node, outside your job. NVLink / PCIe / EFA checksums transport Verify bytes arrived as sent, not that they were computed correctly. Checkpoint checksums storage round-trip A poisoned-but-consistent checkpoint checksums fine. The way to catch SDC is to check the result of the computation itself. Detect: Three checks in your training loop name a suspect GPU by comparing data-parallel replicas. Step 2. title: Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: AI agents and applications that answer questions about recent events, product releases, prices, or regulations need information newer than their model’s training data. Until now, Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore delivered that information to agents through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. That means creating a gateway and a web search target and calling the tool from an MCP client. The setup fits platform teams that share one search policy across many agents, but it’s more than you need when your own code only requires search results. Today, we’re announcing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With it, your own code can search the web with a single API call. It returns ranked results from a web index that Amazon operates, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. You call it from the AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), signed with the same AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials you use for your other AWS services. There are no resources to create first. Authenticate, call, and get results. Use it in an application, an agent loop you write yourself, or a data pipeline. Why a standalone API? The AgentCore Gateway is the recommended path for most agentic workloads. It gives agents one secure Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that combines web search with your other tools. It also handles inbound and outbound authentication, semantic tool selection, and optional MCP sessions . But developers told us they also need a lower-level integration point for scenarios where the gateway is not the right fit: Custom orchestration frameworks – Developers building their own agent loops, or using frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex, want to call web search directly as a tool within their orchestration logic rather than routing through a gateway. Non-agent use cases – Not every application that needs web grounding is an agent. Search-powered dashboards, fact-checking pipelines, content enrichment workflows, and monitoring systems all benefit from real-time web results without requiring agent infrastructure. Tighter control over the request lifecycle – Some developers want to manage retries, caching, and error handling themselves rather than delegating to the gateway. Simpler integration for existing applications – Applications that already have their own API layer can call the Web Search API directly, adding web grounding without adopting the full AgentCore Gateway stack. The Web Search API complements the gateway. It runs on the same search infrastructure that powers Alexa+, Kiro, Quick, and other Amazon products, with the same quality and compliance posture, exposed as a direct API operation. How it works The Web Search API is the InvokeWebSearch operation on the bedrock-agentcore data plane, the same endpoint that other AgentCore tools such as AgentCore Browser , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, use. Requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) from your standard AWS credentials, so there’s no API key or secret to manage. Figure 1: How a Web Search API request flows The numbered steps are: Your application calls InvokeWebSearch with the AWS SDKs or the AWS CLI, which sign the request with SigV4 using its AWS credentials. From a virtual private cloud (VPC), the call can go through an interface VPC endpoint. The API checks with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) that the caller has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch on the AWS managed web search tool. The API applies the filters in the request: the domains to include or exclude and the publication time range. The API searches a web index that Amazon operates. Queries are served inside AWS and aren’t sent to a third-party search engine. The API returns up to maxResults ranked results, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. abstract: At AWS, we believe AI builders should be able to choose the right model for every task, trust their agents in production, and see clearly what their AI workloads cost. That belief guides how we invest across our portfolio. Amazon Bedrock gives you access to leading models and the tools to build and scale AI applications securely. We extend this foundation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , which provides the platform to build, connect, and optimize agents using any model and any framework. That includes Strands , our open source agent development toolkit. Together, they take you from first prototype to production. As agents move into core business workflows, the bar rises. You need the flexibility to use different models as tasks, budgets, and latency targets change. When a primary model is throttled or unreachable, your agents must keep working. They also must act within limits you set and return output other software can use as is. Their answers must stay grounded in sources you allow, and their cost must hold up at high volume. What we shipped in October addresses each of these needs. New models help you match each task to the right price and speed, from high-volume subagents to real-time voice. title: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track
abstract: From November 30th to December 4th, Amazon Web Services (AWS) will hold its annual premier learning event: re:Invent . At this event, attendees will become stronger and more proficient in various areas of AWS technology through a variety of experiences: keynotes given by AWS leaders, interactive working sessions led by AWS experts, and fun, immersive activities such as live entertainment and games at re:Play . There are over 2,000 learning sessions that focus on specific topics at various skill levels, and the AI/ML (AIM) track has more than 140 unique sessions for you to choose from. We’re here to help you identify the sessions that best fit your needs. Even if you can’t join in person, you can catch up with many of the sessions on demand and even watch the keynotes live. The basics: Session types If you can join us, then remember that we offer several types of sessions that can help maximize your learning in a variety of AWS topics. re:Invent attendees can choose to attend breakouts, chalk talks, builder sessions, workshops, and code talks. The breakout sessions are recorded and uploaded a few days after to the AWS Events YouTube channel , while the rest are live non-recorded interactive sessions. Here are the details for each session type: Breakout sessions: Attendees are in a lecture-style 60-minute informative session presented by AWS experts, customers, and partners. Chalk-talk sessions: Attendees interact with presenters, asking questions, and using a whiteboard in session. Builder sessions: Attendees participate in a one-hour session and build something. Workshop sessions: Attendees join a two-hour interactive session where you work in a small team to solve a real problem using AWS services. Code talk sessions: Attendees participate in engaging code-focused sessions where an expert leads a live coding session. Lightning talk sessions: Attendees watch a 20-minute demo dedicated to either a specific service or customer story (located in the Venetian Expo Hall or Wynn/Encore Upper Convention Promenade). With so many sessions to pick from, it helps to know how the pieces fit together. Here is how AWS thinks about its AI offerings, so you can decide where to begin and where to focus. The AWS AI stack overview and tie-in to re:Invent sessions AWS offers a comprehensive AI portfolio in the cloud. It covers everything from the physical infrastructure and AI chips that power AI workloads up through ready-to-use agentic solutions that teams can adopt today. Understanding how these services work together helps you navigate re:Invent and focus on the sessions most relevant to what you’re building. Figure 1: The AWS AI stack Global Infrastructure – It all starts with data centers designed and optimized for AI workloads. These facilities are built to handle the power, cooling, and networking demands that large AI training and inference jobs require. AI Chips – Running inside those data centers are two compute options: AWS Trainium , purpose-built for high-performance AI training and inference, and NVIDIA GPUs for teams that need GPU-based acceleration. Customers choose based on their workload, performance requirements, and cost targets. Data Foundation – AI is only as good as the data behind it. AWS Context connects your data across storage, databases, analytics, and search services, giving models and agents access to the right information at the right time. Models, Training, and Inferencing – This is where models get built, trained, fine-tuned, and served. Amazon Bedrock gives you managed access to hundreds of leading models from multiple providers through a unified API. Amazon SageMaker AI gives you full control to train, fine-tune, and deploy custom models on dedicated infrastructure. Many customers use both depending on the workload. Agent Development and Management – Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is where you build, deploy, and manage AI agents. It supports any model or provider mix, including models from both Amazon Bedrock and Sag

title: Automating AWS Agent Registry updates with push-based architecture
abstract: Every time a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server published in the AWS Agent Registry, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, gains a new tool or updates its schema, the registry record must be updated too. Without automated push-based sync, consumers discover stale metadata. For organizations managing multiple MCP servers across accounts, such a sync keeps catalog records current within an existing governance workflow. In most enterprise deployments, a catalog’s value depends on its freshness. If a developer deploys a new tool on Monday, but the registry record still reflects last week’s schema, consumers lose trust in the catalog. Stale metadata directly reduces registry reliability, leading teams to inadvertently build dependencies on inaccurate information. When an engineer adds a tool to an MCP server but forgets to update the catalog: Consumers miss out on the new capability entirely. Applications might call the tool using an outdated schema, causing unexpected runtime behavior or silent workflow deviations. Multiplied across teams, this lack of automation erodes trust in the registry. Organizations ultimately fall back on ad hoc discovery mechanisms like hardcoded endpoints, informal knowledge sharing, and stale documentation. In this post, we outline an event-driven architecture that automates these updates using AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Lambda. Architecture overview The following solution brings these services together into an event-driven pipeline that detects runtime changes and synchronizes them to the registry automatically. The architecture supports both multi-account and single-account environments: Single-account setup: For straightforward deployments, all components reside within Account A. Cross-account forwarding setup isn’t needed as events flow directly within Account A. Multi-account setup: This involves two accounts where runtime events from Account B are securely forwarded to Account A. Account A (registry account) owns the AWS Agent Registry, the Amazon EventBridge rule, the push-sync Lambda function, and CloudTrail logs. Account B (MCP server account) hosts the MCP server runtime and the Amazon Cognito OAuth provider used for authentication. The sample uses two accounts, but you can scale the architecture for multiple accounts, with Account A as the registry account and multiple AWS accounts similar to Account B for different MCP servers. The following diagram shows the end-to-end event flow for an update to an MCP server in Account B. The captured event is forwarded to Account A, where a Lambda function queries the MCP server for its tools and updates the matching registry record. Figure 1: End-to-end event flow for a cross-account MCP server update, from the CloudTrail event in Account B to the registry record update in Account A. The architecture uses five AWS services: AWS CloudTrail captures UpdateAgentRuntime API calls as management events. Amazon EventBridge routes matching events to the Lambda function, with cross-account forwarding supported. AWS Lambda queries the MCP server for its current tools, diffs against the registry, and updates the record if changed. AWS Agent Registry stores MCP server records and their tool schemas as the central source of truth. AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, brokers OAuth token exchanges securely, so the Lambda authenticates without storing secrets. How it works: business logic flow After it’s deployed, the pipeline runs the following end-to-end workflow: Trigger : A developer in Account B updates an MCP server, which calls the UpdateAgentRuntime API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS CloudTrail captures the event. Route : Amazon EventBridge catches the CloudTrail event and forwards it to the central event bus in Account A . title: How DXC Technology built a multi-model AI substrate on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: This post is co-written with Nick Tamburro of DXC Technology. When an AI agent can act on a production server at a bank or a hospital, access to a capable foundation model is only the starting point. Recent public incidents, in which autonomous agents took destructive actions their operators never intended, show that the real risk is rarely the model alone. It’s an agent holding more authority than its task requires, with nothing in the architecture to stop it. Avoiding that starts with a substrate that governs model access at the infrastructure level. Amazon Bedrock provides that substrate. Through a single managed interface, it gives DXC OASIS access to multiple foundation models: Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova , Meta Llama, and open-weight families. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforce content filtering, personally identifiable information (PII) redaction, and denied-topic policies uniformly across every model. AWS PrivateLink keeps inference traffic within the customer’s virtual private cloud (VPC), and serverless scaling avoids self-managed GPU infrastructure as a failure point. Because these are system-level controls rather than bolt-ons, they gave DXC Technology a governed foundation for what no model layer can deliver on its own: a trusted harness that orchestrates, governs, and audits AI agents across enterprise IT operations at scale. Model availability varies by AWS Region. See Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . DXC Technology runs managed IT services for some of the world’s most regulated organizations: banks, hospitals, and government agencies. With more than 115,000 employees across 70 countries, DXC operates mission-critical systems where resilience and governance are non-negotiable. When DXC set out to build DXC OASIS, the harness for mission-critical IT operations, the team separated the problem into two layers. The first is a governed model substrate built on Amazon Bedrock. The second is the trusted harness built on top: DXC’s own orchestration, governance, and assurance layer. In this post, we explore how DXC built the resilient, flexible model substrate beneath DXC OASIS on Amazon Bedrock. We also show where DXC drew the line between what the substrate provides and what the harness must provide. Since general availability in March 2026, DXC OASIS has reduced resolution time by 95% on average across 56 measured use cases. Across every model, customer data stays within the AWS data boundary: prompts and completions are not shared with third-party model providers and are not used to train the underlying foundation models. “Our customers operate complex, business-critical environments and need both choice and resilience in how they adopt AI. Amazon Bedrock provides access to a broad ecosystem of models with the governance, security, and operational controls required at enterprise scale. That flexibility allows us to use the right model for the right task, adapt as technology evolves, and stay focused on delivering measurable business outcomes for our customers.” — Dan Gray, President, GIS, DXC Technology Solution overview DXC OASIS separates the question of which model from the question of how work gets done. Amazon Bedrock is the substrate: a governed gateway to foundation models (FMs), reachable through one consistent API, with security and networking controls that keep traffic inside the AWS perimeter. The harness is everything DXC builds on top: orchestration across tools and systems, operational context drawn from 60 years of runbooks and escalation logic, policy enforcement, human-oversight gates, and full auditability of every agent action. The design goals were: Resilience: No single point of failure at the model layer. Flexibility: Route each task to the most appropriate model on cost, latency, and capability. abstract: Language model (LM) alignment improves model outputs to reflect human preferences while preserving the capabilities of the base model. title: Agent Substrate: Advancing Kubernetes for Agents at Scale
abstract: AI agents spend most of their time idle, waiting on a human prompt, a tool result or a model response. Kubernetes wasn’t built for that. Running one Pod per... title: Skipper, Airbnb’s embedded workflow engine, is now open source
abstract: Durable workflows, running inside your service with no separate orchestration cluster. By : Ricardo Gamba , Andriy Sergiyenko Skipper , an embedded workflow engine used in production by teams all across Airbnb, is now available to the open source community. Skipper lets you express multi-step business processes as Java or Kotlin classes, persist their progress, and recover from crashes and transient failures. It runs inside your service and reuses its existing dependencies. Skipper is available under the Apache 2.0 license. The code is on GitHub , alongside documentation and runnable examples. Our earlier engineering deep dive explains how we built it. Here, we’ll focus on the architecture of Skipper and where it fits in the ecosystem of options for development around workflows. Why we developed Skipper A process that spans multiple services, waits for human input, or involves a mix of synchronous and asynchronous steps, needs persistent storage for recording its progress. When a server restarts, it must know what has already happened, what (if anything) should be retried, and what is still awaiting processing. Implementing this separately for each process would mean repeatedly solving the same problems around partial failure, timers, and recovery, with associated testing and debugging; using a proven library is likely to improve quality and reduce toil. Existing workflow engines meet these challenges. A common approach relies on a central orchestration service, whether self-hosted or fully managed, to handle durable execution. This setup provides a unified platform for multiple teams, streamlining central operations and monitoring. For Airbnb, we wanted a new approach, one in which each service owned its workflows within its existing deployment and database. For critical services, that meant avoiding an additional shared orchestration dependency. It also let workflow execution stay in-process, without a separate coordinator between steps. That requirement shaped Skipper’s architecture, as shown in the figure. With Skipper, the service’s replicas also run the workflow runtime and scheduler. In a typical production deployment, they share a database that holds workflow state and scheduled work. The scheduler polls for runnable tasks and uses leases to coordinate ownership. If a replica fails, another can recover the work; takeover timing depends on scheduling and lease settings. This reduces the number of separately deployed systems. It also puts responsibility for workflow execution, database capacity, and recovery with the service’s team. The duty of assuming those responsibilities is part of the tradeoff. We believe that Skipper will appeal to teams that have a robust operational environment and need a workflow engine that adapts to their existing ways of working. A workflow is a class Skipper has two main abstractions. A workflow describes the orchestration: decisions, ordering, and waits. Actions perform work with potential side effects, such as calling an API or updating a database. Skipper records action results so they can be reused during recovery. Consider a hypothetical listing-publication process. Some listings require a human review before publication; afterward, the host receives a notification: class PublishListing : Workflow() { private val listing = actions<ListingActions>() @StateField var reviewApproved: Boolean? = null @WorkflowMethod suspend fun publish(request: PublicationRequest): Boolean { if (request.requiresReview) { val reviewed = waitUntil( { reviewApproved != null }, Duration.ofDays(1) ) if (!reviewed || reviewApproved != true) return false } listing.publish(request.listingId, request.requestId) listing.notifyHost(request.listingId, request.requestId) return true } @SignalMethod fun recordReview(approved: Boolean) { reviewApproved = approved } } waitUntil hibernates the workflow without holding a thread. The recordReview signal lets an API handler or queue consumer supply the review decision. A redep

Generative AI in the Real World: Memory for Personal AI with Duncan Davidson
abstract: This post was created with the assistance of AI, based on a transcript of the conversation. AI tools have started to remember their users, but each tool remembers a different version of the same person. Duncan Davidson, an independent consultant and longtime software engineer, has been trying to connect those fragments. He joined Ben Lorica to discuss what personal AI could do if people could carry their context between services and decide what each service gets to see. They also talked about how AI coding changed web development during Duncan’s time at Webflow, what new developers may lose as entry-level work changes, and why open source projects need new ways to handle AI-assisted contributions. About the Generative AI in the Real World podcast: In 2023, ChatGPT put AI on everyone’s agenda. In 2026, the challenge will be turning those agendas into reality. In Generative AI in the Real World , Ben Lorica interviews leaders who are building with AI. Learn from their experience to help put AI to work in your enterprise. Check out other episodes of this podcast on the O’Reilly learning platform or follow us on YouTube , Spotify , Apple , or wherever you get your podcasts. Takeaways 06.31 The developer’s job is moving toward outcomes. Duncan compared AI coding to desktop publishing, which removed the physical work of assembling pages but left designers responsible for what the page should look like. At Webflow, he saw people use AI tools to make websites faster than they could with earlier tools. For developers, he said, the question has shifted from how quickly they can type code to “What outcome do you want? What are you trying to do with this code, and how can you make it better?” People still need to judge whether an implementation fits the rest of the system. 10.41 New developers still need a way to become experts. Computer science fundamentals still matter when an agent offers several plausible fixes and a person must choose the one that fits a larger system. Ben asked where future engineers will gain that judgment if AI absorbs entry-level tasks. Duncan compared early career work to an apprenticeship in the arts, where even menial assignments expose newcomers to how the whole operation works. Companies that measure only throughput, he warned, may leave too little room for people to learn. 23.07 AI-assisted changes are straining open source review. Duncan described a library he uses in one of his apps. His fixes, along with performance problems Claude noticed, left his version roughly 25 pull requests ahead of the project’s main branch. The maintainers were using AI too, he said. The difficulty was getting useful changes back to the project without overwhelming its review process. His conclusion was that older open source collaboration practices need a “serious retrofit.” 28.27 Personal memory is fragmented across tools. Duncan first had his coding agents save useful information into a collection of Markdown files. Once commercial agents added memory, he found that “Claude knew me one way and ChatGPT knows me another way.” He could push context back to each tool with instructions and occasional reminders, but that solution demands more tinkering than most people want to do. What he wants is a small set of shared mechanisms that let a person carry context across services. 34.01 Portable memory needs boundaries. A prompt’s context, an agent’s memory of recent interactions, and a person’s longer-term knowledge should be able to travel, but Duncan also wants people to control access by scope. He keeps general notes alongside information about his family and finances. His test for a useful system is whether he can say, “Give Claude access to these scopes of my knowledge, but not everything.” That becomes harder when a personal agent encounters knowledge gained at work. title: Why Git Needs Help: Moving from Files to Systems for Source Control
abstract: The shift to agentic reality When Git was designed in 2005, Linus Torvalds solved a brilliant problem for humans collaborating over terminal windows by trading line-by-line diffs. Fast-forward to 2026: Autonomous coding agents don’t think in flat text files or line breaks. They reason across syntax trees, execution traces, call graphs, and type constraints. In my view, forcing an AI agent to engineer complex distributed systems through string matching is like handing a chief software architect a chisel and a stack of sticky notes. File-centric versus system-centric paradigm shift Dimension Legacy file-centric (Git) Agent-native system graph Representation Flat Unicode text streams Tree-Sitter ASTs & CPG nodes Mutation unit Line-by-line string diffs AST node transformations Context overhead 2,000+ line prompt context fills Sub-50 token targeted node payloads State persistence Ephemeral model prompt windows Execution ledgers & reasoning chains Whenever I see engineers try to lock context-blind models into file-centric version control, I watch the consequences compound quickly. Context windows fill with irrelevant churn, API bills surge, and subtle, multifile structural breakages slip past basic syntax checks. Just as critically, standard Git discards the cognitive history of a change. The moment an agent session completes, its execution logs, compiler feedback, and discarded hypotheses evaporate into thin air. Tactical illustration: renaming a distributed method signature Consider updating a core helper signature across 40 dependent services. A traditional string diff forces the agent to read and mutate thousands of lines of surrounding boilerplate text, burning thousands of context tokens per file: --- a/services/auth.py +++ b/services/auth.py @@ -42,7 +42,7 @@ class AuthManager: def validate_session(self, token: str) -> UserSession: - return fetch_user_by_token(token) + return fetch_user_by_token(token, include_metadata=True) In contrast, an AST mutation node isolates the target function symbol, executing the change precisely without passing unneeded ambient text through the prompt window: { "action": "mutate_node", "target_ast_id": "ast_node_89f2a41b", "symbol": "fetch_user_by_token", "update": { "add_argument": { "name": "include_metadata", "value": true } } } This exact bottleneck hit Anthropic in late 2026. As autonomous agent activity pushed monorepo merges beyond 30,000 per day, conventional Git infrastructure simply buckled under the load. To me, unlocking genuine agentic autonomy requires evolving source control along two complementary tracks: shifting to server-hosted, graph-aware architectures, and treating agent reasoning as a first-class, versioned artifact right alongside the code itself. Why text diffs and ephemeral sessions create silent debt Standard diff tools operate purely on raw Unicode strings. When an agent reorders functions or cleans up formatting, string diffs pollute context windows with noise while remaining blind to structural reality. If you modify a single method signature, Git won’t warn you about the dozen callers broken across separate modules. From my experience, feeding 2,000-line source files into prompts just to update a 5-line helper method degrades model attention, burns compute, and inflates overhead at scale. Text diffs versus AST graph mutations Metric / behavior Text diff (unified patch) AST graph mutation Formatting resilience Breaks on whitespace or line-ending changes Immune to syntax formatting shifts Impact analysis Post hoc CI test failures Sub-second static call-graph resolution Token consumption O(file_size) per prompt iteration O(node_delta) per targeted change Compounding this structural blind spot is what I consider our biggest waste: ephemeral session memory. Whenever an agent finishes a task or compacts its context window, its entire diagnostic history—failed attempts, shell outputs, and compiler warnings—disappears. title: Where Are the “Killer Apps” of AI?
abstract: Most of today’s AI entrepreneurs and social media enthusiasts are young. AI is the first technology revolution they’ve lived through. They don’t remember how unbelievably exciting it was in the late 1970s to get your own computer, instead of struggling to get time on one of the vast machines chugging away in what used to be called “the glass house,” an air-conditioned room where from outside you could watch the nine-track tapes being accessed and the refrigerator-sized disk drives spinning. Input and output was on high-speed teletype printers (no screens) and magnetic tape (and before that on punch cards.) They also mostly don’t remember, as I do, writing assembly-language programs in which you moved data from one computer register to another, specified the arithmetic or logical operations to be performed on it, and then specified where to save the result. They look at today’s AI and marvel at how virtually anyone can now generate code. They don’t realize that that’s also how it felt when you could use an interpreted programming language like BASIC to write your own applications instead of writing them in Assembler. They also don’t remember when Dan Bricklin used BASIC to write the first version of VisiCalc in 1979. He went into business with Bob Frankston, who rewrote it in 6502 Assembly Language for the Apple II. Dan was able to express the idea in Basic; Bob then wrote a tight, efficient version for widespread distribution. People rushed out to buy computers so they could use VisiCalc, and everyone predicted that the VisiCalc “spreadsheet” would put all the accountants out of work. It was the first program to be referred to as a “killer app.” It wasn’t the democratization of programming itself that was the killer app but what Dan and Bob did with it. In the entrepreneurial explosion that followed, databases, graphics, word processing, and other business applications came out of the glass house and, as Bill Gates put it, “onto every desk and into every home.” Dan Bricklin (right) with Bob Frankston, who rewrote VisiCalc in 6502 Assembly Language for the Apple II Image from https://www.digitec.ch/en/page/visicalc-the-first-killer-app-in-computer-history-16230 We saw the same leap from astonishment to innovation to adoption with the World Wide Web. When O’Reilly demonstrated GNN , the first commercial website, to people at a trade show in 1993, attendees couldn’t believe that clicking on a link could pop up an image or a document from another computer thousands of miles away. They didn’t understand the difference between the software application (the web browser) from the network-connected documents with clickable hyperlinks that it acted as a frame for. They didn’t understand that web pages were a new kind of software written in a simple markup language anyone could understand. It didn’t make sense that the web page was a document that in many ways could look and act like a kind of program. And when people did understand, they thought that might be the end of programming. In 1993, everyone thought that the web browser itself was the killer app, and that Marc Andreessen, the young creator of Mosaic, the most popular web browser, which became Netscape, was going to dethrone Bill Gates as the new king of computing. They didn’t realize that the true killer apps of the web were not the web browser and the web server but applications “up the stack” built using the new programming paradigm the web enabled. Those applications weren’t software as we’d known software before. They were database- and application-backed websites delivering services that were previously impossible. I remember thinking of Amazon as the 2005 equivalent to VisiCalc when a friend told me she had just bought her first computer so she could shop on Amazon. Once again, it wasn’t the new capability itself that was the killer app but what developers did with it. What makes a killer app? title: Measuring AI’s Unintended Consequences
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. AI is great for making teams faster. But is it sustainable? What about maintainability, burnout, and lock-in? This is part 3 of my series on assessing AI’s impact on software development. In part 1 , we looked at why assessing impact is important, and what not to do. In part 2 , we looked at how to measure AI’s impact on delivery speed. In this part, we’re looking at how to measure and model the unintended consequences of using AI. Then we’ll wrap up in part 4 with an examination of business outcomes. Finally, an epilogue puts it all together with notes you can share with your CFO. Does maintainability even matter? I can hear it now: “Who cares about namby-pamby issues like maintainability and burnout? It’s a job. If jobs were supposed to be fun, they wouldn’t be called ‘work!’ Suck it up!” So let me be clear: We care about AI’s unintended consequences because they have real economic impact. If code isn’t maintainable, features take longer to write and bugs take longer to fix, taking time away from more valuable work. If people are burned out, they don’t put forth their full effort, and they eventually quit, taking institutional knowledge with them and leading to time-consuming hiring cycles. If you’re locked in, and AI token costs increase, you could be stuck with a choice between a big bill and cutting back on development. Among the people I’ve talked to, there’s widespread agreement that heavy use of AI produces code that humans have trouble understanding. But there’s disagreement about how much that matters. If AI is doing the maintenance, do we care if a human can understand the code? There are strong opinions on this topic on all sides, but not a lot of actual evidence. What’s clear is that the costs of maintenance and other unintended consequences do matter, but only if there are any costs. This is what we need to measure: Is there an impact? And if there is, is it enough to matter? Unfortunately, unlike the rigorous speed trial we discussed in part 2 , unintended consequences are gradual and fuzzy. Your measurements are going to be noisy and lagging. You’ll have to create models and explore scenarios. Ultimately, your decisions will come down to judgment, informed by your measurements and models but not driven by them. One ring to rule them all There is one idea that, while not perfect, does a good job of capturing the majority of unintended consequences. It’s cost of change . Put simply, cost of change is like a tax on the changes you make to your software. When cost of change is low, complicated changes still take time, but they’re achievable. When cost of change is high, even simple changes can take weeks, and complicated changes seem completely out of reach. Cost of change isn’t easy to measure, but there are several indicators you can use to inform your judgment. Value-add percentage Value-add percentage is the percentage of your software development effort that’s spent on things that bring value to your business, such as new features, versus the percentage of effort that’s spent on non-value-add work, such as fixing bugs, resolving incidents, and manual test and release cycles. Non-value-add work is called “muda.” 1 Some muda is necessary, even valuable, but that doesn’t make it value-add. Imagine a demanding and crotchety customer who always asks, “Why didn’t you just do it right the first time?” If that customer won’t pay for something, it’s muda. That’s why bug fixes are muda: “I’m not paying you to fix a bug that shouldn’t be there in the first place!” And performing releases: “Why don’t you just ship it already! How hard can it be?” Sure, bug fixes can be valuable, and releases are necessary, but they’re still muda. I find it useful to distinguish muda further into discretionary and nondiscretionary muda. Discretionary muda is work that you choose, such as inves

title: Human-Pilled
abstract: The following article originally appeared on the Asimov’s Addendum Substack and is being republished here with the author’s permission. This essay is based on my conversation with Demetrios Brinkmann for AAIF Live, recorded before my keynote at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose on October 23, 2026. It was edited and rearranged for publication by Ilan Strauss, and in places it draws on the keynote. Both videos are also on the AI Disclosures Project website in the new “Missing Mechanisms” page. The keynote begins at 1:28:40 in the Day 2 livestream . The Bitter Lesson vs. AI Markets for Human Expertise In 2019, the computer scientist Richard Sutton wrote a short essay called “ The Bitter Lesson .” Looking back over 70 years of AI research, he concluded that general methods that scale with raw computation beat methods built on human expertise, and by a large margin. The AI industry as a whole is bitter-lesson-pilled, to borrow the internet’s slang for a true believer. I am human-pilled. I believe in the bitter lesson. Brute force wins out in the end, and I have wrestled with that fact throughout my career. But we humans still have to figure out our role in the AI economy, and I find it rather disturbing that the AI community isn’t spending more time asking how to make this future friendlier for humans. The labs think about how to keep AI from going rogue, and their chief economists study job losses from AI. They don’t study what mechanisms we could introduce to create new economic opportunities for humans. The question matters to us at O’Reilly Media. We don’t think of ourselves as a publisher, a conference producer, or an online learning platform so much as a company that transfers knowledge from the people at the cutting edge to the people who want to follow them. So we are very interested in what human expertise is worth, even in the face of AI. Knowing everything and nothing Human expertise was used to train AI, which makes AI a fabulous cultural technology . Thousands of years ago, the only knowledge people had was what they could keep in their heads. Since then we have built better and better ways to share knowledge across time and space, and AI continues that. With each of these transitions, we have to ask again what the truly human is still worth. People often say judgment, or taste. That’s true, but I think it goes deeper: AI is a sea of possibility. All of that knowledge sits in the model, and nothing sets it in motion except a human. (That is changing a little as we start giving AI agents long-running tasks, and we will have to come to grips with it.) If you and I used Claude or ChatGPT for the same research project, we would each bring different experience to it, tell it what we want and why, and give it context in different ways. I see that as the unique focusing power of human consciousness and attention. Earlier this year I spent an hour or so talking this question over with Claude. When it offered to write up a first draft for me, I said no. I wanted an essay from its own point of view about what it took away from our conversation. The result, “ Why AI Needs Us ,” opens, “He came in through Powys,” and a few paragraphs later says, “The choice of entry point was already the argument.” That captured what I’m getting at. I had come into the conversation through a book I love, John Cowper Powys’s The Meaning of Culture , which distinguishes culture from education. Powys gives his own unique and powerful definition: “Culture is what is left over after you have forgotten all you have definitely set out to learn.” It is what you absorbed. Each of us absorbs a small and particular slice of everything. Large language models (LLMs) try to absorb everything, and so become overly general; we give them focus. Human knowledge provides them with a lens. Let me bring that into a business context. title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
abstract: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers. The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
abstract: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey. COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20. This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31. In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked. This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations. Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.” So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage. Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.) The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country). Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal. Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support. One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there. title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud. Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be . —Antonio Regalado This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI —Grace Huckins As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times. “We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it . The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity —James O’Donnell As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape. Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback. title: Evolving metal extraction processes
abstract: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible. Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize. Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations? EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted: “We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.” A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on. Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience. That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions. Beyond optimization For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways. The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential. Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT. “The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. title: When Does It Actually Make Sense to Put AI Into Products?
abstract: Over the past few years, the tech industry has rushed to plug a new microchip into every device on the assumption that if you can add AI, you should. Smart-vision toothbrushes , mood-reading household robots , and a host of physical products are invading consumers’ daily lives, reliant on artificial intelligence to learn, predict, and adjust our behavior. But as anyone who’s struggled to update the firmware in their fridge knows, AI doesn’t improve every product. Some product designers are asking where the line is between genuine innovation and a solution looking for a problem. Savannah Kunovsky leads a team of industrial product designers at Ideo , a design consultancy based in San Francisco focused on helping clients unpack when AI becomes a barrier rather than a breakthrough. Kunovsky spoke with IEEE Spectrum about the pressure to integrate AI in everything, where that integration goes wrong, and what companies can do to determine when an AI integration is—and isn’t—a smart choice. When AI makes products worse How much of the current wave of AI integration into physical products is driven by pressure from investors and shareholders to keep up with industry trends? Savannah Kunovsky : Some of it. Teams come to us feeling pressured to show they’re doing something with AI, sometimes because a CEO has promised the board an “AI story” before the next earnings call, or a competitor has just launched an AI-powered version of their product. In all cases, the first thing we do is step back and ask who the product is for and what they’re trying to do. Once that’s clear, the role AI should play, whether large, small, or invisible, usually becomes obvious. There is an appetite for this kind of grounding in the industry right now. People want to cut through the hype and see what works in practice. How do you distinguish between a genuinely helpful AI feature and a gimmick? Kunovsky : The test for an AI gimmick is the same test we’d apply to any product experience: Does it help someone do what they’re trying to do? Answering that means understanding how people would use the product in the real context they’ll be using it. Many companies look straight to large language models (LLMs) because that’s top of their mind, but there is a whole AI toolbox to draw from: computer vision, sensor fusion, on-device models, et cetera. Picking the right capability for the task matters as much as deciding whether to use AI in the first place. As a new interaction paradigm, AI is asking people to change their behavior, so it needs to be simple. When IDEO’s predecessor firm worked on Apple’s first mouse in the early 1980s , the team gave it only one button because people were learning a completely unfamiliar system and the interaction mechanism needed to be effortless. The wearable Humane AI pin used projection instead of a screen-based display, making a dramatic shift from the smartphone interface users already know. Angel Garcia/Bloomberg/Getty Images In which products has AI made the user experience worse? Kunovsky : The clearest examples are products where AI replaced something that already worked. I have a lot of respect for Humane’s AI Pin as a provocation, but the technology [a screenless, wearable smartphone alternative that uses an AI assistant instead of apps] wasn’t ready . The Pin asked people to give up an interface they knew well for one that was slower and less reliable, which is a hard trade-off to ask of anyone. You see versions of this problem everywhere—a voice assistant that mishears a simple command and turns off the wrong light, a customer service bot that keeps you in a loop when you just want a person. In cars, climate and volume controls moved onto touchscreens and voice menus, so something you used to do by feel now takes your eyes off the road. title: NSF’s X-Labs Program Draws Support From Charities and Investors
abstract: When the U.S. National Science Foundation began its X-Labs program in May, the agency said the higher-risk, higher-funded awards would create new kinds of partnerships that would confront urgent scientific and technological challenges. Now the NSF is doubling down on the idea, with an announcement in October that charities, companies, and investment funds would provide X-Lab winners practical support such as laboratory space, software, shared equipment, and access to key data and expert guidance. The help provided by these organizations, which the NSF is calling “ consortium partners ,” will not give them ownership stakes in the X-Labs projects. The addition of the consortium partners may help the initial winners—who will be announced later in November or December and receive US $1.5 million for a 9-month planning phase—reach the aggressive targets needed to compete for much larger $50 million multiyear grants. “It’s a way of telling X-Labs applicants you don’t need to reinvent the wheel, so you’re not spending half of your X-Labs money to go build or buy basic infrastructure,” says Matt Cimaglia , an investor in consortium partners Occam Foundry and Florida Quantum Center . NSF X-Labs Focus on AI, Computing, and More The NSF initially announced two focus areas for the X-Labs program: scientific instruments for sensing and imaging and photonic microchips for quantum systems . In September, the agency followed up with three additional areas in AI for physical devices , decoding biological sequences , and pushing the physical limits of computing . The NSF requires potential X-Labs award recipients to eventually demonstrate autonomy : Leaders for projects must be focused on the work full-time, for example, and must be able to make hiring and spending decisions independently from any university or commercial owners. That agility sets X-Labs apart, along with the risk appetite. Consortium partners saw the potential to provide infrastructure and operations support to allow X-Labs recipients to focus on research. “[We’re] very interested in the enabling structures of R&D,” says Joshua M. Greenberg , program director at the Sloan Foundation, one of the participating partners. Greenberg says that the foundation has supported multiple focused research organizations, or FROs, already. FROs are independent entities in the same vein as what the X-Labs program hopes to create. Unlike university laboratories or larger tech companies, FROs are founded with a time-limited purpose of advancing research in a well-defined area. Because they start with a clean slate, FROs may lack the infrastructure that university or corporate research groups might inherit. To address that lack of infrastructure, bioengineering service firm Ginkgo Bioworks , in Boston, is offering X-Lab winners up to $5 million worth of access to its “cloud lab,” says Jason Kelly , the firm’s CEO and founder. Ginkgo’s cloud lab can conduct complex and flexible laboratory work, and the company will also offer laboratory space and internal datasets that could be useful for training AI models. Kelly is enthusiastic about the potential for X-Labs, which he says have the potential to “pull platforms into existence” like the federal Human Genome Project once did, which enabled a lot of subsequent innovation. As scientific and technology companies become more powerful, Kelly says, it’s natural that governments should revisit how to involve them in government-led science. “The scale of companies is not like it was in the Vannevar Bush era [in the 1940s],” he says, “so how should the United States leverage those [much larger, more capable] companies? It’s silly to leave them on the sidelines.” In 1945, Vannevar Bush wrote an influential report that helped shape the modern NSF and U.S. federal science funding. title: In reversal, American Cancer Society urges prostate cancer tests for all men
abstract: In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that all men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA test. Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday. Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years. title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
abstract: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. Read full article Comments

title: Ars Live: What drone attacks on data centers mean for modern life in the cloud
abstract: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki , a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans. Read full article Comments

You say you've bought all of the roughly 5,000 re-releases and remasters of Skyrim that have been made available in the last 15 years? You weren't there day one back in 2004, Nokia N-Gage in hand , ready to experience the game's 176 x 208 resolution mobile hack-and-slash RPG combat for yourself?
